title: Nonprofit Board Financial Reports: What Your Board Should See Every Month
summary: Nonprofit board financial reports should show cash, results against budget and restricted money. Learn what goes in the monthly package and what to ask.
body_markdown:
## What Financial Reports a Nonprofit Board Should See


Nonprofit board financial reports come down to six documents, each one answering a question the board is accountable for answering.


In order: the statement of financial position, the statement of activities against budget, cash with the months of operating cash on hand, restricted grant balances, the functional expense split across program services, management and general and fundraising, and a one-page narrative of the variances. Ask what financial reports should a nonprofit board review and the honest answer is usually fewer than the packet already contains.


The list is short for a governance reason. Board members are fiduciaries, and the National Council of Nonprofits describes the duty of care as ensuring “prudent use of all assets, including facility, people, and good will.” The duty of obedience covers whether the organization “obeys applicable laws and regulations, follows its own bylaws” and holds to its stated purposes ([Board Roles and Responsibilities](https://www.councilofnonprofits.org/running-nonprofit/governance-leadership/board-roles-and-responsibilities) ). Donor restrictions sit inside that second duty. So does the budget this board approved.


A board package isn’t a performance review of the finance team. It’s the evidence a board needs to discharge duties it already carries.


### Each report and the oversight question it answers


Report in the package The oversight question it answers What a good answer looks like


Statement of financial position Can we meet our obligations, and how much of what we hold is ours to spend on general operations? Net assets split with and without donor restrictions, current assets covering current liabilities, no unexplained growth in payables


Statement of activities against budget Are we on the plan this board approved, and if we aren’t, does management know why? Year-to-date actual beside year-to-date budget, with every line past the board’s variance threshold carrying a written explanation


Cash and months of operating cash on hand Can we make payroll and cover the next twelve months without touching restricted money? Cash excluding donor-restricted and board-designated amounts, trended across three months, plus a short forward projection


Restricted grant balances Are we spending each grant inside its stated purpose and inside its period? Award, spent to date, remaining and period elapsed for every grant, with any grant trailing its period flagged


Functional expense split Can we show donors, funders and the IRS how their support was actually used? Program services, management and general and fundraising, year to date, in categories that map to Form 990 Part IX


One-page variance narrative What should this board discuss and decide this month? Named variance, named cause, named action, named owner, reviewed by the treasurer before the packet goes out


The statement of financial position goes first because every figure after it reads differently once the board knows what the organization holds and owes.[ASU 2016-14](https://storage.fasb.org/ASU_2016-14.pdf) requires net assets in two classes, with and without donor restrictions, replacing the three classes before it. Detail on the statement lives in our guide to the[nonprofit statement of financial position](https://www.indinero.com/blog/nonprofit-balance-sheet/) , and the classes in[net assets with and without donor restrictions](https://www.indinero.com/blog/net-assets-in-nonprofit-accounting/) .


Two things belong on a different cadence. The statement of cash flows is required in the annual GAAP statements, and quarterly is usually enough for a board. And any organization approaching the federal single audit threshold needs one watch line, because the test under[2 CFR 200.501](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-2/section-200.501) is federal awards expended during the fiscal year, not awarded or received.


## How to Build the Monthly Board Financial Package


A board package gets built in a fixed sequence that starts with a closed month, not with a report template.


If the month isn’t closed and the accounts aren’t reconciled, every figure downstream is a draft, and nonprofit financial reporting to the board becomes a debate about whether the numbers are right.


1. **Close the month and reconcile every account.** Bank accounts, credit cards, investment accounts and payroll liabilities. Unreconciled cash is the most common reason a package gets reissued, which is why[account reconciliation](https://www.indinero.com/blog/what-is-account-reconciliation-a-brief-guide-for-business-owners/) is the gate on everything after it.
2. **Code contributions by restriction as they land.** Gifts, grants and pledges get classified with or without donor restrictions when they’re recorded, not sorted out at year end. Releases get recorded in the month the restriction is satisfied.
3. **Allocate functional expenses for the month.** Payroll, occupancy and shared costs split across program services, management and general and fundraising. The[Instructions for Form 990](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i990) allow an organization whose system doesn’t allocate expenses to use any reasonable method. Reasonable, documented, and consistent month to month are the three words that matter.
4. **Update the restricted grant schedule from the closed books.** One row per grant, pulled from the ledger rather than kept in a side spreadsheet that drifts.
5. **Produce the statements with a budget column.** Year-to-date actual, year-to-date budget, variance in amount and percentage, and the annual budget for context.
6. **Write the one-page variance narrative.** Staff writes it, against the threshold the board itself set. Anything over that threshold gets a sentence naming the cause, the action and the owner, and anything the narrative can’t explain gets flagged as unexplained rather than smoothed over.
7. **Finance committee review.** The treasurer and the finance committee see the package before the full board does. Their job at that stage is to find the questions, not to correct the arithmetic.
8. **Distribute several days ahead.** A package handed out at the table gets skimmed, and a skimmed package produces a motion to accept with no oversight behind it.


A nonprofit board financial dashboard belongs at the front of that package, not in place of it. One page of trends, the cash ratio and the grant spend-down, with the statements behind it.


One separation is worth writing into the finance committee’s charge. Accounting staff or an outsourced team owns the close, the reconciliations, the allocation and the statements. The executive director reviews before distribution, the treasurer before the board.[Preparing for a nonprofit audit](https://www.indinero.com/blog/how-prepare-nonprofit-audit/) is the organization’s work, and the opinion belongs to the independent auditor.


Monthly close, monthly package to the finance committee, the full six reports at every regular meeting. A board that meets quarterly still needs monthly closes behind it, because a quarterly close shows a problem already a quarter old. Budgeting and the wider practice sit in our guide to[nonprofit financial management](https://www.indinero.com/blog/nonprofit-financial-management/) .


## A Worked Example: One Month’s Board Package for a Fictional Organization


Riverbend Youth Collective is a fictional organization, invented for this walkthrough, and every figure below is a percentage or a ratio.


It’s a 501(c)(3) with a June 30 fiscal year end, three programs and three active restricted grants. The package is for January, month seven, so 58 percent of the fiscal year has elapsed. The finance director prepares it, the executive director reviews it, and the finance committee meets a week before the board.


**Statement of financial position.** Total net assets are up 4 percent since July 1.[Net assets with donor restrictions](https://www.indinero.com/blog/net-assets-in-nonprofit-accounting/) are 38 percent of the total, up from 31 percent. Current assets cover current liabilities 2.1 to 1.


**Statement of activities against budget.** Revenue and support is at 51 percent of the annual budget with 58 percent of the year gone, 7 points behind. Expenses are at 52 percent. The change in net assets is slightly ahead of budget, which is the first thing a reader notices and the last thing to act on.


**Cash.** Cash excluding donor-restricted and board-designated amounts covers 2.6 months of average monthly expenses, down from 3.4 months at July 1, and down in each of the last three months.


**Functional split, year to date.** Program services 76 percent, management and general 14 percent, fundraising 10 percent, allocated monthly on the method in the organization’s cost allocation policy.


Restricted grant Spent to date Grant period elapsed


Grant A, after-school programming 72 percent 67 percent


Grant B, summer learning expansion 18 percent 50 percent


Grant C, capacity building 100 percent Closed


### The variance that looks alarming and isn’t


Grant B is the frightening row. Eighteen percent spent against half the grant period elapsed reads three ways, all of them bad. The program isn’t delivering, the money is about to be lost, or somebody has lost track of the grant.


None of those is true. Grant B funds a summer program, the grant period runs January through December, and the spending concentrates in June through August when the program actually operates. Two things follow from that one fact. The expense underrun is a timing difference, and the 7-point revenue shortfall is the same timing difference seen from the revenue side, because the release of those net assets follows the spending that satisfies the restriction. The budget assumed a straight-line twelfth each month. The grant doesn’t work that way.


One timing difference, two frightening numbers.


### What the finance committee does with it


The committee’s job isn’t to be reassured. On Grant B it tests the explanation. Is the spending window still achievable, what is the planned spend by month, does the agreement permit a no-cost extension, and is the straight-line assumption worth fixing so this row stops raising a false alarm every month.


Then it moves to the figure that deserves the hour. Months of operating cash fell from 3.4 to 2.6 over seven months, and in each of the last three. The question isn’t why cash is down. It’s show us the next twelve months. Which month is the trough, and does the projection assume any restricted money is available for general operations, because it isn’t.


The recommendation is one motion with a date on it. Management brings a twelve-month cash projection and a draft reserve policy to the next meeting. What the committee skips is the change in net assets sitting slightly ahead of budget, because a board that stops at the combined total would have called this a good month.


## Common Board Reporting Mistakes and How to Fix Them


Most weak board packages fail in one of eight ways, and most are fixed by changing a template rather than by hiring anyone.


None of this is carelessness. Finance teams in small organizations are short on capacity, and a template nobody has had time to rebuild quietly sets the agenda for every meeting.


1. **The default system report, unmodified.** Sixty expense lines, no budget column, no restriction split, no subtotals a non-accountant can use. Build a board-facing version with summary categories, a budget column and the two net asset classes, and keep the detailed version for staff.
2. **Calling the result net income.** The GAAP measure is the change in net assets, reported by class. A board told “net income” asks whether the number is big enough. A board told “change in net assets without donor restrictions” asks whether the organization can fund general operations.
3. **Collapsing restricted and unrestricted results into one total.** An organization can post a healthy total change in net assets in a month when the money available for general operations shrank. ASU 2016-14 requires the two-class presentation so that difference stays visible. Report the change in each class, every month.
4. **Reporting a single cash number.** One balance that mixes restricted gifts, board-designated reserves and operating cash overstates liquidity. Report cash available for general operations separately, and compute the ratio on that conservative figure.[Reconciling the bank account](https://www.indinero.com/blog/why-is-it-important-to-reconcile-your-bank-account/) first is what makes the figure trustworthy.
5. **No variance narrative.** Without one, the meeting becomes someone reading line items aloud while the board waits for the part where it reacts. One page. Variance, cause, action, owner.
6. **The package arrives at the meeting.** Write a standing distribution deadline into the finance committee’s charge so it survives a change in staff.
7. **Functional expenses allocated once a year.** Allocating program, management and general, and fundraising costs only at audit or filing time means the board has never seen the split it’s being asked to vouch for. Allocate monthly, and keep the package’s categories aligned to Form 990 Part IX. That monthly split is also what[accounting infrastructure contributes to fundraising](https://www.indinero.com/blog/accounting-supports-nonprofit-fundraising/) conversations with donors.
8. **Treating a reserve benchmark as a rule handed down from outside.** The board adopts its own written reserve policy, which is the subject of the next section.


A ninth failure is harder to template away. The package is complete, accurate, on time, and it never leads to a decision. When three straight meetings produce nothing but a motion to accept, usually nobody has told the board which question each report is there to answer.


## The Oversight Questions a Treasurer and Finance Committee Should Ask


A treasurer’s value isn’t in the arithmetic. It’s in the five or six questions that turn a set of statements into a decision.


A nonprofit treasurer report is that oversight layer, not a second set of statements. The statements say what happened. The report says what it means and what the committee recommends.


- **From the statement of financial position.** Can we pay what we owe in the next ninety days from assets we’re free to use? Has anything moved in a way nobody can explain?
- **From the statement of activities against budget.** Which variances are timing and which are performance? Is the change in net assets without donor restrictions positive, and if not, for how many months?
- **From cash.** Can we make payroll for the next twelve months without using restricted money? Which month is the low point, and what assumption is the projection most dependent on?
- **From the restricted grant schedule.** Which grant’s spend rate trails its period elapsed, and is there a written plan with dates? Is any funder report due in the next ninety days?
- **From the functional split and the narrative.** Would a donor, a funder and the IRS get the same answer from this split? And what is management worried about that isn’t in a number yet?


### The reserve question, and why there’s no number to quote


ASU 2016-14’s liquidity disclosure frames this conversation. It calls for qualitative information on how an organization manages its liquid resources, plus quantitative information on the availability of financial assets to meet cash needs for general expenditures within one year of the balance sheet date. Writing in The CPA Journal, Curtis Klotz, CPA, notes that assets become unavailable for that disclosure when they carry “donor restrictions or carry board designations,” along with limits such as “a minimum cash reserve required by a loan covenant” ([Nonprofit Liquidity](https://www.cpajournal.com/2020/05/29/nonprofit-liquidity/) ).


Read that from the board’s side. Board designations reduce availability, the board is the only body that creates them, and the standard calls for disclosing their amounts and purposes. The availability figure in the notes is partly a product of the board’s own decisions.


So treat any benchmark as input. The Nonprofit Operating Reserves Initiative Workgroup suggested a minimum operating reserve ratio of 25 percent, roughly three months of the annual operating expense budget, and that same workgroup concluded there is no one-size-fits-all ratio, recommending instead that every organization adopt a written policy setting its own adequate level and recording the rationale behind it ([Operating Reserve Policy Toolkit](https://weingartfnd.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Operating_Reserves_Policy_Toolkit_1st_Ed_2010-09-16.pdf) ). The Greater Washington Society of CPAs Educational Foundation puts the caveat plainly: “An organization needs to determine what its own healthy reserve ratio is,” and the 25 percent minimum “may not be adequate for groups with high revenue volatility and/or less or no controllable expenses” ([Operating Reserve Ratio](https://www.nonprofitaccountingbasics.org/internal-reporting/operating-reserve-ratio) ).


The board sets the number.


The same CPA society publishes the monthly ratio as cash on hand divided by total annual expenses divided by twelve, computed by excluding restricted funds, board-designated reserves and endowment, and reads under 3 or a downward trend as possible cause for concern ([Ratio: Months Cash on Hand](https://www.nonprofitaccountingbasics.org/internal-reporting/ratio-months-cash-hand) ). That’s interpretation guidance from a CPA society, not a requirement.


### Finance committee and audit committee aren’t the same job


The finance committee reviews the monthly package, the budget and the forecast, and recommends to the board. The audit committee oversees the independent audit. In its Nonprofit Audit Guide, the National Council of Nonprofits calls an audit committee a board committee “tasked with the authority to oversee the independent audit process” that “is not involved in the nonprofit’s daily accounting functions,” and notes that where a separate committee is impractical the role may be delegated to another standing committee or to the full board ([Board’s Role and Audit Committees](https://www.councilofnonprofits.org/running-nonprofit/nonprofit-audit-guidec/boards-role-audit-committees) ). If one committee carries both jobs, name them separately in its charge. Reviewing management’s numbers and evaluating the auditor who tests those numbers are different kinds of work.


### What Form 990 Part VI asks about board review


Line 11a asks whether the organization provided a complete copy of the Form 990, as ultimately filed, to every member of its governing body before filing. Line 11b requires a description on Schedule O of the review process, if any. All filers answer both, and the instructions note that federal tax law does not itself require the governing body to review the return. So line 11b is a public description of the organization’s own governance. A board that has seen the functional split every month isn’t meeting its[Form 990](https://www.indinero.com/blog/understanding-form-990/) Part IX figures for the first time in filing season.

## Frequently asked questions


Boards that change their reporting tend to land on the same handful of questions. Here’s how we answer them for executive directors, finance teams and treasurers.


### How often should a nonprofit board review financial statements?


A nonprofit board should review financial statements at every regular board meeting, with a closed and reconciled month behind each report. Nothing in federal tax law sets a review cadence, so your bylaws and board policies govern. A board that meets quarterly should still receive three monthly packages rather than one quarterly roll-up, because a quarterly close shows a problem that is already a quarter old.


### What is the difference between the treasurer’s report and the financial statements?


The treasurer’s report interprets the numbers and recommends action, while the financial statements are the underlying GAAP reports prepared from closed books. The treasurer or finance committee chair walks the board through what changed and what needs a decision, and the statements are the evidence behind that narrative. A board needs both, and the treasurer’s report should never replace the statements themselves.


### Should the board see results with and without donor restrictions separately?


Yes, the board should see the change in net assets with and without donor restrictions separately, because a combined total hides operating capacity. FASB ASU 2016-14 requires the statements to present net assets with donor restrictions and net assets without donor restrictions for exactly that reason. A strong month funded entirely by a restricted grant is not a strong month for payroll, so show both columns and the total.


### What is a budget variance report and why does the board need one?


A budget variance report compares actual results to the approved budget line by line, with a written reason for every material difference. Your board needs it because approving a budget is a fiduciary act, and variance reporting is how the board learns whether that plan is holding. Most variances are timing rather than trouble, and a restricted grant recognized in a different month than it is spent is the most common cause.


### Who should prepare the board financial package?


Finance staff or an outsourced finance team should prepare the board financial package, and the treasurer and finance committee review it before the board. The board doesn’t prepare its own package, because preparing and overseeing the same document collapses the oversight, and your executive director should see it before distribution. Indinero closes the books every month and prepares board-ready reporting your team approves before it goes out.


### What should the finance committee review before the full board meets?


The finance committee should review the complete package before it reaches the board agenda, confirming the month is closed and every account reconciled. From there the committee reads the statements against budget, tests cash and the availability of financial assets for the next twelve months, and reviews restricted grant balances. The committee’s job is to shorten the board’s work to decisions and exceptions, and to send organization-specific questions to your auditor or counsel.
